lines: A job gets re-run, purely to fix one small bug, over the exact same data as before.
The number it reports for a day that's already closed books quietly shifts, by just a sliver. Nobody touched a single row of the underlying data.
Same input, same fix. So what else, hiding somewhere, actually disagreed?
Worth reasoning through before the reveal settles it.
The input going in is confirmed to be exactly the same both times. Something else, buried in the logic itself, clearly wasn't.
What's the one kind of thing that could quietly sneak into a calculation like that?
answer: Not the data. Something living inside the calculation's own logic.
Maybe it secretly asked what time it was right now. Maybe it quietly leaned on whatever order rows happened to arrive in. Maybe it sampled something without ever fixing a starting point.
Any one of those turns an identical rerun into a different answer, even though nothing about the underlying data moved at all.

lines: Two separate properties, together, are what actually make rerunning something safe to trust.
One: feed it the exact same input, and it hands back the exact same output, every time, with nothing else sneaking in.
Two: write the same result twice, and nothing extra happens the second time around.
Run a properly fixed version twice, and both runs land on the exact same answer, every time.
Run a version still hiding a quiet clock-check inside it, and the second run lands somewhere slightly different. That gap between the two is the bug itself, now impossible to miss.
Picture a single moving line, constantly asserting: everything up to right here has fully arrived.

That's a working guess, not an unbreakable promise. Anything that still shows up after that line has already moved past it counts as late, by definition — and someone now has to decide what happens to it.
With no plan at all for that lateness, a late arrival simply vanishes. Gone, with nobody the wiser.

Build in a proper window for correcting things, and that exact same late arrival instead quietly updates what was already published — carrying a brand new version alongside it, never silently writing over the old one.
How wide that correction window actually needs to be comes straight from a real, measured rate of how often things show up late.
A wider window is never a free safety cushion. It means holding onto more state for longer, and it means a number people already saw can keep shifting under them more often.
Every single thing this pipeline ever publishes should carry its own tag: exactly which version of the logic, and which cut of the data, produced it.
A correction adds on a fresh version instead of ever quietly erasing what came before.
That alone is what lets someone downstream lock onto one specific version, and lets someone auditing it later rebuild exactly what was reported, and precisely when.
A trustworthy rerun comes from two properties working together, not either one alone.
A moving line names what counts as late. A proper correction window updates things instead of quietly dropping them.
And carrying a version on everything published is what finally lets anyone lock onto, or later rebuild, exactly what was said.
One more, to use this for real: this same pipeline also fires off a receipt by email, as a pure side effect.
Making the pipeline's own writes safe to redo — does that safety automatically reach all the way out to that email too?
answer: No. Making one system's own writes safe to repeat says nothing at all about a completely separate system sitting outside it.
Without its own way of recognizing a repeat, rerunning the pipeline just quietly fires that same email off a second time.
The fix has to live at the side effect itself. It can't simply be assumed just because the pipeline upstream of it is already correct.
